In algebra, given a [[differential graded algebra]] ''A'' over a [[commutative ring]] ''R'', the '''derived tensor product''' functor is
:<math>- \otimes_A^{\textbf{L}} - : D(\mathsf{M}_A) \times D({}_A \mathsf{M}) \to D({}_R \mathsf{M})</math>
where <math>\mathsf{M}_A</math> and <math>{}_A \mathsf{M}</math> are the [[category of modules|categories of right ''A''-modules]] and left ''A''-modules and ''D'' refers to the homotopy category (i.e., [[derived category]]).<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Hinich|first=Vladimir|date=1997-02-11|title=Homological algebra of homotopy algebras|arxiv=q-alg/9702015 }}</ref> By definition, it is the left derived functor of the [[tensor product of modules|tensor product functor]] <math>- \otimes_A - : \mathsf{M}_A \times {}_A \mathsf{M} \to {}_R \mathsf{M}</math>.

== Derived tensor product in derived ring theory ==
If ''R'' is an ordinary ring and ''M'', ''N'' right and left modules over it, then, regarding them as discrete spectra, one can form the smash product of them:
:<math>M \otimes_R^L N</math>
whose ''i''-th homotopy is the ''i''-th [[Tor functor|Tor]]:
:<math>\pi_i (M \otimes_R^L N) = \operatorname{Tor}^R_i(M, N)</math>.
It is called the '''derived tensor product''' of ''M'' and ''N''. In particular, <math>\pi_0 (M \otimes_R^L N)</math> is the usual [[tensor product of modules]] ''M'' and ''N'' over ''R''.

Geometrically, the derived tensor product corresponds to the [[intersection product]] (of [[derived scheme]]s).

'''Example''': Let ''R'' be a [[simplicial commutative ring]], ''Q''(''R'') → ''R'' be a cofibrant replacement, and <math>\Omega_{Q(R)}^1</math> be the module of Kähler differentials. Then
:<math>\mathbb{L}_R = \Omega_{Q(R)}^1 \otimes^L_{Q(R)} R</math>
is an ''R''-module called the [[cotangent complex]] of ''R''. It is functorial in ''R'': each ''R'' → ''S'' gives rise to <math>\mathbb{L}_R \to \mathbb{L}_S</math>. Then, for each ''R'' → ''S'', there is the cofiber sequence of ''S''-modules
:<math>\mathbb{L}_{S/R} \to \mathbb{L}_R \otimes_R^L S \to \mathbb{L}_S.</math>
The cofiber <math>\mathbb{L}_{S/R}</math> is called the relative cotangent complex.
